item.title: Is It Intuition, or Is It Anxiety?
item.description:
Intuition

Is It Intuition, or Is It Anxiety?

Intuition and anxiety arrive as a felt sense, but they move in opposite directions.

Posted August 19, 2026

Key points
  • Intuition and anxiety are both forms of bodily knowing, which is precisely why they often get confused.
  • Jung classified intuition as a mode of perception, whereas anxiety can signal an activated survival state.
  • The reliable difference is not content but movement: intuition opens; anxiety narrows.

Some version of this question surfaces in my clinical consulting room nearly every season: "How do I know if this is my intuition, or if it's just my anxiety?"

The person asking is usually experiencing a major moment in their life where something in them has been speaking to them, but they simply cannot tell what that is.

Jung’s Intuition

In Jung's typology, intuition sits alongside sensation, thinking, and feeling as one of four functions of consciousness.1 Notice what Jung did not do: He did not classify it as an emotion. He classified it as a legitimate mode of perception, specifically a way of experiencing the world by way of the unconscious.

This distinction matters clinically. Where the sensation function of the psyche reports what is going on through one’s five senses, intuition reports where something is going. So, intuition apprehends pattern, trajectory, or "big picture" thinking, so to speak, and latent possibility. Intuition hands you the whole before you have assembled the parts, which is why it so often arrives as a unique type of knowing without a concrete paper trail. An intuitive person often cannot tell you how they know something, but they simply just know through a hunch, dream, or sudden realization.

Jung associated the intuitive function with the psyche's forward-moving, teleological intelligence: the aspect of us oriented not toward what has already happened, but toward what is trying to happen. In this way, we can approach intuition as an invitation into the realm of creative possibilities for what can exist within a person’s life.

Source: Photo by Anthony Tran on Unsplash

Anxiety

Anxiety is frequently the signature of an activated complex: an emotionally charged constellation organized around an old injury in the human psyche and body. When a complex constellates, the mind begins to perceive threat, whether real or imagined, and the human nervous system naturally braces itself accordingly. The field of vision quickly narrows to the perimeter of the threat.

Anxiety is so convincing because it carries genuine energy, real bodily urgency, and often a compelling narrative. Some expressions of anxiety can be highly logical, and I often joke with people in my practice that their anxious mind could out-think even the most intelligent philosophers. However, anxiety doesn’t carry new information for people and more so acts like an alarm system, because it’s fundamentally built from past negative experiences, repetition, and/or old traumatic wounds that is being projected onto the future.

Put plainly: Intuition is the psyche perceiving, whereas anxiety is the survival wisdom of the mind and body protecting itself.

The Difference

When clients and I slow this down together, we can spot some observable differences which tend to hold up across cases.

  • Direction: Intuition opens. There is a widening quality to it, a sense that the world has more doors in it than you previously counted. Anxiety constricts; it closes doors until only one remains, and that one is usually marked as some fearful version of "do not move”.
  • Tempo. Intuition tends to arrive once, quietly, and then wait for you. Intuition does not argue, whereas the anxious complex repeats, escalates, and builds a case. If the voice has a prosecutor tone, it is probably not intuition.
  • Relationship to time. Intuition is strangely present tense, even when it concerns the future; it feels like recognition in the moment. Anxiety lives almost entirely in a rehearsed future, running simulations of some type of catastrophe, and is often experienced as an overwhelming spiral.
  • Somatic quality. Clients describe intuition as warmth, spaciousness, and an embodied type of settling. Anxiety announces itself as tightening in the chest, jaw, or gut, with the breath going high and shallow. The body knows the difference well before the mind does.
  • Relationship to the world. This one is the most reliable in my experience. Intuition carries a quality of connection: to the moment, other people, and to something larger than the egoic self. In contrast, anxiety isolates, and sometimes generates the peculiar loneliness of being the only person who can see the perceived danger.
  • Aftertaste. Intuition tends to leave a person steadier, even when the outcome is difficult and the variables remain unknown. Anxiety tends to leave a person needing reassurance again within the hour, then again, and then again. Reassurance behaves like sugar on an empty stomach: genuine relief, followed by a crash that returns the person hungrier than before.

The Spiritual Dimension

Since transpersonal psychology emerged as a named field at the end of the 1960s, its psychologists and writers have treated intuition as a legitimate mode of knowing rather than a lesser one. Across that literature, intuition appears in strikingly different registers: as genuine insight into the nature of reality, as the wellspring of scientific discovery and artistic inspiration, as fundamentally mystical, and, more colloquially, as picking something up from the "vibe" of a room.2

What unites these accounts is a claim about structure rather than speed. Intuition is not merely faster cognition, but a deep moment of participation within existence itself: a moment in which the ordinary boundary between self and world becomes briefly permeable.

That is why genuine intuition so often carries a note of awe or presence rather than urgency. Anxiety produces the opposite experience, not because it drives people away from others, but because it generates the peculiar loneliness of being the only one who can see what threat is coming, which often inflicts a felt sense experience of disconnection.

item.title: Why People Are More Honest With AI Than Their Own Boss
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

Why People Are More Honest With AI Than Their Own Boss

New research complicates what we thought about AI, trust, and speaking up.

Posted August 19, 2026

Key points
  • People are more willing to speak up to AI leaders than human ones.
  • AI feels fairer to many employees, which unlocks psychological safety.
  • The effect holds for cognitive tasks but disappears for emotional ones.
Turns out the robot might be the easier one to talk to.
Source: Enchanted Tools / Unsplash

A post published here last December made a compelling case that AI will never truly lead. The argument was essentially that leadership is deeply nonverbal. Posture, eye contact, warmth, the trembling voice, genuine shame—all of these communicate things an algorithm can’t experience. And without that, it cannot lead.

It's a reasonable argument. And then a study came out last month that made it more complicated.

What New Data Found

Researchers at Zhejiang University conducted three separate experiments testing how willing employees were to speak up, raise concerns, and offer honest feedback to algorithmic leaders versus human ones (Wang et al., 2026). The study, published in Scientific Reports, produced consistent findings across all three experiments.

People were significantly more willing to voice honest opinions to an algorithmic leader than to a human one.

The researchers traced the effect to perceptions of fairness. Employees saw algorithmic leaders as fairer, which was associated with greater psychological safety, the sense that they could speak up without paying a social cost. That, in turn, was associated with more honest communication.

The effect was specific. For cognitive tasks such as decision-making, performance evaluation, and resource allocation, the algorithmic leader elicited more honest input than the human one. For emotional tasks, the effect disappeared entirely. Nobody found it easier to be emotionally vulnerable with a machine.

The Uncomfortable Question

The study doesn’t settle the question of whether AI can lead. But it does expose something uncomfortable about human leadership.

If people are more honest with an algorithm than with their own boss, the interesting question may have less to do with algorithms than with human leadership. What happens in a workplace when employees associate honesty with social risk?

People are speaking up to algorithms because they are afraid of what happens when they speak up to people. A manager remembers the moment you pushed back. They may unconsciously favour people who agree with them. They may even carry that impression into your next performance review. An algorithm doesn’t have those same social relationships with its employees.

What matters here may not be that the leader is an algorithm. It may be that employees don’t perceive the same social risks when they speak to it.

What AI Reveals About Human Leadership

The December post argued that AI lacks the moral fabric of leadership. That's worth thinking about. An algorithm can identify an optimal decision. It can’t experience the weight of making it.

But the study raises a different question for human managers: What does it mean if employees are more comfortable being honest with an algorithm than with you? It may be a sign that your team has learned to associate honesty with risk.

The finding doesn’t suggest that human leaders should be replaced by machines. Instead, it gives managers an uncomfortable question to consider: What are we doing, consciously or otherwise, that makes people hesitate before they speak?

Whatever the answer is, it probably has more to do with human leadership than with better algorithms.

AI may lack the emotional qualities we associate with leadership. Yet for some employees, it appears to create enough psychological safety for them to say what they really think.

The irony is not lost.

The question of why we trust AI differently doesn’t stop at the workplace. It is part of a broader question about how we decide what—and whom—to take seriously online.
